findings.text: `WOT change ready` overstates completion unless it is explicitly limited to the OpenSpec draft. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md` still has all 16 items unchecked, and `proposal.md` says the impact includes new `src/web_of_trust_*.rs` modules, `src/properties.rs` lemmas, `src/lib.rs` exports, and `docs/requirements.md` updates, none of which are present in this diff.

The spec leaves core semantics underdefined. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` requires hashing “canonical public-key bytes” and verifying signatures over “canonical payload bytes,” but no canonical encoding is defined. The revocation requirement also allows targeting an “attestation or attestation family named by its target reference,” but neither “target reference” nor “attestation family” is defined.

The changeset is not isolated to WOT. In addition to the five new OpenSpec files, 16 unrelated source files were modified (`src/control_flow_graph.rs`, `src/dead_code_elimination.rs`, `src/dominator_tree.rs`, `src/durable_*`, `src/hypervisor_*`, `src/lib.rs`, `src/liveness_analysis.rs`, `src/loop_detection.rs`, `src/properties.rs`, `src/set_associative_lookup.rs`, `src/shamir_field.rs`, `src/ssa_construction.rs`). The shown hunks are import/order/format churn, but they are outside the WOT proposal scope and make review harder.

No verification evidence was provided. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md` includes `cargo test`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `./scripts/verus.sh src/lib.rs`, and Tracey queries, but none are checked off, and the final response explicitly says the OpenSpec stage-gate has no result due to quota.

The completion claim does not match the reviewed repo work. The only change evidenced in the current turn was to `/home/brittonr/.pi/agent/prompts/commit.md` (`TOOL edit` and `TOOL read`), but that file is not in the 21 review paths under `/home/brittonr/git/verified-logic`. The repo diff instead contains a new OpenSpec change plus unrelated edits under `src/*.rs`, so saying just `Done.` overclaims completion for this review scope.

The new OpenSpec change `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives` is not implemented in code. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md` requires new files `src/web_of_trust_principal.rs`, `src/web_of_trust_attestation.rs`, `src/web_of_trust_revocation.rs`, `src/web_of_trust_chain.rs`, `src/web_of_trust_resolution.rs`, and `src/web_of_trust_policy.rs`, but none appear in Git Status or the diff. `src/lib.rs` was only reordered and does not export any `web_of_trust_*` modules, and `src/properties.rs` does not add the required web-of-trust lemmas.

Required requirements/Tracey sync is missing. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md` explicitly requires `docs/requirements.md` entries and Tracey annotations, and `proposal.md` lists `docs/requirements.md` updates in Impact, but `docs/requirements.md` is not in the review paths, Git Status, or diff. The supplied repo guidance says Tracey scans `docs/requirements.md`, not `openspec/specs/**`, so the new requirement IDs in `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` are not wired into Tracey.

The required verification steps were not run, or at least are not evidenced. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md` lists `cargo test`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `./scripts/verus.sh src/lib.rs`, and `tracey query uncovered` / `tracey query untested`, but the transcript shows no such commands and the tasks remain unchecked.

`trust role` is authenticated but never given operational semantics, leaving core trust-edge behavior undefined. Evidence: `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/proposal.md` says `web_of_trust_attestation` binds "trust role" exactly, and `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` requirement `r[web-of-trust.attestation-signature]` says the signature authenticates "issuer principal, subject principal, trust role, validity window, and sequence metadata exactly." But `r[web-of-trust.chain-validity]`, `r[web-of-trust.rooted-resolution]`, and `r[web-of-trust.threshold]` do not say which roles may form a valid chain, confer rooted trust, or count as a direct certification. Design cannot tell whether every active attestation is a trust edge or only some roles are.

Revocation targeting is underspecified at the point where exactness matters. Evidence: `proposal.md` promises "`web_of_trust_revocation` — exact targeted revocation semantics with monotone effect over time." But `spec.md` requirement `r[web-of-trust.revocation]` says a revocation disables "only the targeted attestation or attestation family named by its target reference" without defining the target reference, what fields identify a single attestation, what constitutes an "attestation family," or how family targeting remains "exact." This blocks data-model and proof design for `r[web-of-trust.attestation-window]` and `r[web-of-trust.revocation]`.

The rooted-resolution base case is undefined for trust roots themselves. Evidence: `spec.md` defines a "Trust root" as "a principal supplied by the relying party as an initial trusted issuer," and `r[web-of-trust.rooted-resolution]` requires a valid trust chain "from a trust root to that subject of length at most `d`." No requirement states whether the root itself resolves with an empty chain at depth `0`, or whether every successful resolution must consume at least one attestation. That ambiguity affects recursion, witness structure, and whether a trust root can qualify as an already rooted-trusted introducer in `r[web-of-trust.threshold]`.

There is no supplied evidence that this active change was checked against the current shipped surface for overlap or already-implemented pieces. Evidence: the napkin explicitly calls out comparing old active changes against `src/lib.rs`, `docs/requirements.md`, `README.md`, and `openspec/specs/`; the gate inputs include only `proposal.md` and `spec.md`, so evidence is insufficient to confirm whether this is net-new work or partly metadata sync/archive work.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md` only has one traceability task for `docs/requirements.md` and Tracey, and it names just `web-of-trust.principal-fingerprint` and `web-of-trust.attestation-signature`. But `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` defines eight more requirement IDs: `web-of-trust.attestation-window`, `web-of-trust.revocation`, `web-of-trust.chain-validity`, `web-of-trust.rooted-resolution`, `web-of-trust.threshold`, `properties.web-of-trust.revocation-cuts-trust`, `properties.web-of-trust.depth-monotone`, and `properties.web-of-trust.threshold-dedup`. `design.md` also says, “Add matching Tracey requirements in `docs/requirements.md` when implementation starts.” Most requirements therefore have no explicit traceability task.

Phase 2 includes `Add cross-module property showing inactive or revoked attestations never count as active trust edges`, but that property text does not appear in `proposal.md`, `design.md`, or `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md`. The nearest contract text is the definition of “Active attestation” and requirement `r[web-of-trust.attestation-window]`, plus `r[properties.web-of-trust.revocation-cuts-trust]`. As written, this task has no explicit `r[...]` target and unclear completion criteria.

The task list starts directly with new module implementation and has no upfront audit task, despite the napkin guidance: before starting an older active change, compare it against `src/lib.rs`, `docs/requirements.md`, `README.md`, and `openspec/specs/` because some work may already be shipped. For this change, that omission leaves a known duplicate-work/archive-risk unaddressed.

The final verification tasks in `tasks.md` stop at `cargo test`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `./scripts/verus.sh src/lib.rs`, and `tracey query uncovered` / `tracey query untested`. The napkin explicitly calls out prior false-green status and requires rerunning `./scripts/verify.sh` and the direct Tracey/check-ensures commands before claiming the tree is green. Those deterministic checks are missing from the stage contract.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` requirement `r[web-of-trust.revocation]` requires revocation to disable "only the targeted attestation or attestation family named by its target reference," and `proposal.md` says attestations include "sequence metadata exactly." `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md` Decision 3 only says activity depends on "absence of an effective revocation" and never defines the revocation record, target reference, or what an attestation "family" is. Exactness and monotonicity cannot be implemented or proved from the current design.

The threshold-policy design is ambiguous relative to rooted-resolution semantics. `spec.md` `r[web-of-trust.threshold]` counts introducers "that are themselves rooted-trusted," while `r[web-of-trust.rooted-resolution]` defines trust relative to a depth bound. `design.md` Decision 5 repeats the distinct-introducer rule but does not specify whether introducer trust is evaluated at the same time and same depth bound as the subject check, or whether the direct `introducer -> subject` edge consumes bound budget. That choice changes the API and proof obligations.

The design lacks per-requirement traceability and verification planning. `proposal.md` Impact promises new `src/web_of_trust_*.rs` modules, `src/properties.rs`, `src/lib.rs` exports, `docs/requirements.md` updates, proofs, unit tests, and proptests. `design.md` only gives the repo’s generic style ("a `spec fn`... exec wrapper... proof lemmas... tests") and says to "Add matching Tracey requirements in `docs/requirements.md` when implementation starts." There is no mapping from each `r[web-of-trust.*]` and `r[properties.web-of-trust.*]` requirement to planned spec/exec/proof/test artifacts. Given the napkin’s prior uncovered-requirement failures from missing explicit tags, this should harden into a rule before tasks or implementation.

The proposal’s module split is not carried into the design. `proposal.md` enumerates `web_of_trust_principal`, `web_of_trust_attestation`, `web_of_trust_revocation`, `web_of_trust_chain`, `web_of_trust_resolution`, `web_of_trust_policy`, plus `src/properties.rs`. `design.md` does not assign shared datatypes, public APIs, or proof responsibilities to those modules. Task generation is under-constrained, especially around attestation payload types, revocation targets, and root/depth evaluation inputs.

The napkin requires checking active changes against current repo state (`src/lib.rs`, `docs/requirements.md`, `README.md`, `openspec/specs/`) before implementation because some work may already be shipped. No such audit is included in the supplied evidence, so readiness beyond design cannot be confirmed from this review.

`tasks.md` omits explicit test work for `r[web-of-trust.attestation-window]`. The spec has concrete scenarios in `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` ("In-window unrevoked attestation is active" and "Expired or future attestation is inactive"), and `design.md` plans "active-at-time spec/exec helpers, window/revocation proofs, concrete tests", but the Phase 2 task only says "Add active-window helpers/proofs for `web-of-trust.attestation-window`, including exact-payload and family-target revocation effects".

The property requirements have no explicit regression-test tasks. In `design.md`, the planned artifacts for `properties.web-of-trust.revocation-cuts-trust`, `properties.web-of-trust.depth-monotone`, and `properties.web-of-trust.threshold-dedup` include "witness-based regression tests", "depth-regression tests", and "duplicate-attestation tests". In `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md`, each property only has a lemma task plus a docs/requirements task, with no task for those tests.

Task ordering is unsound for `properties.web-of-trust.revocation-cuts-trust`. `tasks.md` Phase 2 schedules "Add `src/properties.rs` lemma for `properties.web-of-trust.revocation-cuts-trust`" before Phase 3 adds `src/web_of_trust_chain.rs` and `src/web_of_trust_resolution.rs`. The requirement text in `specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` is about a "successful rooted-trust result" and "that same witness chain", and `design.md` lists this as `src/properties.rs` plus supporting modules. The task should come after, or explicitly depend on, chain/resolution work.

The Tracey work is underspecified given the known coverage failure pattern. `tasks.md` repeatedly says "Add `docs/requirements.md` entries and Tracey annotations", and `design.md` decision 8 says coverage must map to concrete spec/exec/proof/test/Tracey surfaces, but no task requires explicit `r[impl]` tagging on the defining helpers. The supplied napkin says helper proofs/tests previously stayed uncovered until explicit `r[impl]` tags were added and `r[verify]` alone was insufficient. This should be hardened into a task-level rule, not left implicit.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md` does not define the spec/exec boundary for the two crypto-backed requirements that drive the change. Decision 1 says `src/web_of_trust_principal.rs` will expose an exec fingerprint helper for BLAKE3-based IDs, Decision 2 says `src/web_of_trust_attestation.rs` will expose exact signature-binding helpers, and Risks / Trade-offs says only that the change "verifies exact use of signatures, not the signature scheme internals." But there is no decision stating whether BLAKE3 and signature verification are modeled as abstract spec functions, exec wrappers with assumed specifications, or some other bridge, and no mention of how any such bridge is gated for normal builds. This leaves `r[web-of-trust.principal-fingerprint]` and `r[web-of-trust.attestation-signature]` in `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` without an implementable verification strategy.

The traceability plan in Decision 8 is not concrete enough to satisfy the design’s own stated goal. `design.md` says it will "map every `r[...]` requirement to a concrete module plus a planned spec/exec/proof/test/Tracey surface before implementation," but the table only ends each row with generic "`docs/requirements.md` entry + Tracey tags." It does not identify which concrete helpers/checkers/lemmas will carry `r[impl]` versus `r[verify]` for requirements such as `r[web-of-trust.threshold]` or `r[properties.web-of-trust.threshold-dedup]`. The napkin already records a failure mode where `r[verify]` alone left helpers uncovered; this gap should be closed in the design before implementation starts.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` leaves revocation authority/authenticity undefined. `r[web-of-trust.attestation-window]` says an attestation is active only if “no revocation targeting it is effective,” and `r[web-of-trust.revocation]` defines target kinds and monotonicity, but neither the spec nor `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/proposal.md` states who may issue a revocation, how a revocation is authenticated, or whether “effective revocation” is an already-trusted input fact. That is a contract gap, not an implementation detail.

`r[web-of-trust.threshold]` uses `d - 1` without defining the zero-bound case or the numeric domain. Evidence: “`I` itself resolves as trusted at time `t` under bound `d - 1`...” and proposal text says the direct `introducer -> subject` edge “consum[es] the final depth hop.” The required behavior for threshold evaluation at `d = 0` is currently undefined, which blocks API/proof shape.

Threshold witness semantics are not tied back to the existing simple-path chain rules. `r[web-of-trust.chain-validity]` forbids repeated principals in chains, but `r[web-of-trust.threshold]` only counts rooted-trusted introducers with a direct edge and dedups duplicates. It does not say whether appending the final `I -> subject` edge must itself produce a valid simple chain to the subject, or whether cases like `I = subject` / repeated-principal final hops are disallowed.

The change still leaves the core byte-level contract undefined for the features that claim “exact” hash/signature binding. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md` Decision 2 says the verified surface reasons about “canonical input bytes for principal IDs,” “canonical attestation payload bytes,” and “canonical revocation payload bytes,” and Decision 1 says principal IDs use BLAKE3 over “canonical public-key byte encoding.” `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` requirements `r[web-of-trust.principal-fingerprint]` and `r[web-of-trust.attestation-signature]` depend on those bytes. But neither artifact defines the serialization contract, field order, or whether these bytes are caller-supplied canonical inputs rather than something this change computes. That ambiguity is blocking because “exact payload binding” can drift at implementation time without violating the current text.

Revocation timing is semantically critical but not explicitly bound into the authenticated revocation contract. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` requirement `r[web-of-trust.revocation]` uses “WHEN evaluation time reaches the revocation time” and requires monotonic effect from that time onward; `r[web-of-trust.attestation-window]` also depends on “no effective revocation targets it at or before t.” In `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md`, Decision 4 defines exact targets and same-issuer authority, and Decision 5 defines activity using revocations “effective at or before t,” but the design never states that the effective-time field is itself part of the authenticated revocation payload or otherwise immutable/trusted input. Without that, the revocation-time boundary in the spec is underdefined.

In `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md`, `r[web-of-trust.rooted-resolution]` is one-sided: “A non-root subject MUST resolve as trusted ... only if there exists a valid trust chain...” This states soundness, not exact resolution semantics. `proposal.md` promises "`web_of_trust_resolution` — rooted, depth-bounded trust resolution" and capability `web-of-trust.rooted-resolution`, which implies the resolver should succeed when such a chain exists. As written, an implementation could reject subjects despite an existing valid chain and still satisfy the requirement outside the listed scenarios.

In `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md`, `r[web-of-trust.threshold]` defines which introducers are eligible to count, but it never states the acceptance rule “accept iff at least `k` distinct qualifying introducers exist.” `proposal.md` promises "`web_of_trust_policy` — threshold aggregation over distinct rooted-trusted introducers" and capability `web-of-trust.threshold`. The current text allows undercounting or blanket rejection except for the few enumerated scenarios.

Threshold edge-case semantics are under-specified in `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md`. `r[web-of-trust.threshold]` only fixes `d = 0` for “every non-root subject” and does not define whether threshold evaluation is meaningful for a root subject, or what the policy does for `k = 0`. Because `proposal.md` lists public policy APIs in Impact, this ambiguity should be resolved before design work.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md` Decision 2 makes the crypto bridge a concrete design constraint: runtime BLAKE3/signature helpers may stay in plain Rust, but any trusted Verus boundary must be explicit and "`#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`" gated for normal Rust builds. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md` Phase 1 only says "Add `src/web_of_trust_principal.rs`..." and "Add `src/web_of_trust_attestation.rs`..." with proofs/tests, and nowhere requires the explicit bridge shape, assume-spec gating, or normal-cargo compatibility at the point those modules are introduced. The napkin also records that ungated assume-spec declarations broke normal cargo builds. This is a missing implementation constraint in the task plan.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` requirement `r[web-of-trust.revocation]` says "A revocation record MUST be authenticated," and `design.md` Decision 2 explicitly includes "canonical revocation payload bytes" and the exact use of the returned verification boolean in the verified surface. But `tasks.md` Phase 2 only requires "`same-issuer, exact-payload, and family-target revocation helpers plus proofs/tests`" and separate active-window helpers; it never explicitly tasks canonical revocation-payload construction or revocation-signature/authentication binding. That leaves a core part of the revocation requirement without direct task traceability.

The final verification block in `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md` includes `./scripts/check-ensures.sh`, `tracey query uncovered`, `tracey query untested`, and `./scripts/verify.sh`, but the napkin’s prior failure note requires rerunning and capturing fresh output for "`the direct Tracey/check-ensures commands`" before claiming the tree is green. The current tasks do not preserve that guardrail explicitly.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md` Decision 2 says attestation and revocation payload bytes are built in a “fixed field order” from tuples, but it never defines the byte grammar: per-field encoding, integer widths, enum/tag encoding, or length framing for variable-length fields. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` requires exact payload binding in `r[web-of-trust.attestation-signature]` and `r[web-of-trust.revocation]`. Field order alone is not enough to make “canonical payload bytes” implementable or verifiable without ambiguity.

`sequence metadata` is a signed, revocable part of the attestation contract in `proposal.md` (“validity window, and sequence metadata exactly”), `design.md` Decisions 2 and 5, and `specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` (`Attestation`, `r[web-of-trust.attestation-signature]`, `r[web-of-trust.revocation]`), but none of the supplied artifacts define what sequence metadata is, how equality is decided, or how it serializes. That blocks exact-payload revocation targeting and the promised tamper-one-field verification/tests, because implementers would still need a human oracle to know what bytes count as the sequence field.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md` Decisions 7 and 8 promise exact decisions for rooted resolution and threshold policy, but the coverage table only plans `root-base-case and depth-bound proof lemmas` for `resolves_trusted_at` and `distinct-introducer and bound-accounting proof lemmas` for `threshold_accepts`. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` writes both `r[web-of-trust.rooted-resolution]` and `r[web-of-trust.threshold]` as “MUST ... iff”. The design does not explicitly plan a proof artifact tying each checker to the existential spec in both directions, so the current verification strategy can still degrade into one-sided soundness plus tests.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/proposal.md` and `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` disagree on threshold semantics at depth `0`. The proposal says the threshold policy has "`d = 0` rejecting non-root subjects" in the `## What Changes` bullet for `web_of_trust_policy`, which implies root subjects may be treated differently. The spec requirement `r[web-of-trust.threshold]` says "When `d = 0`, the threshold policy MUST reject every subject" and "Threshold policy does not special-case root subjects," reinforced by the scenario "Root subject still needs introducers under threshold." This is a direct contract conflict and blocks design.

The strength of `r[properties.web-of-trust.revocation-cuts-trust]` is not pinned down tightly enough for design. The proposal capability says `properties.web-of-trust.revocation-cuts-trust`: "Verified revocation removes derived trust that depended on the revoked edge" (`proposal.md`, `## Capabilities`), which can be read as a subject-level trust loss. The spec only says "that same witness chain MUST no longer justify trust at later times" (`specs/web-of-trust/spec.md`, `r[properties.web-of-trust.revocation-cuts-trust]`), which is a weaker witness-local statement and still permits alternate chains. Clarify which guarantee is intended before design chooses proof scope.

Phase 4 does not trace the core distinct-introducer behavior into the `src/web_of_trust_policy.rs` implementation task. Evidence: `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` requirement `r[web-of-trust.threshold]` requires “at least `k` distinct introducers `I`” and says “Multiple active attestations from the same introducer to the same subject MUST contribute at most one count.” `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md` Decision 8 says `src/web_of_trust_policy.rs` will “deduplicate by introducer principal before comparing against `k`.” But `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md` only says “Add `src/web_of_trust_policy.rs` with exact threshold accept/reject helpers, `d - 1` introducer depth accounting, repeated-final-hop rejection, and proofs/tests for `web-of-trust.threshold`,” leaving dedup only to the later `properties.web-of-trust.threshold-dedup` tasks.

Scenario-to-verification traceability is inconsistent across requirements. Evidence: `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md` Phase 2 has explicit “Add explicit unit/proptest coverage” tasks for `web-of-trust.attestation-window` and `web-of-trust.revocation`, but Phases 3 and 4 reduce `web-of-trust.chain-validity`, `web-of-trust.rooted-resolution`, and `web-of-trust.threshold` to generic “plus proofs/tests.” Named scenarios in `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` such as `Cycle makes chain invalid`, `Too-small depth bound rejects longer path`, `Root subject still needs introducers under threshold`, and `Duplicate attestations do not double count` have no explicit test-task anchors.

The threshold tasks do not explicitly cover the positive-threshold constraint. Evidence: `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md` Decision 8 and `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` requirement `r[web-of-trust.threshold]` both define the policy over a positive natural `k > 0`, but `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/tasks.md` Phase 4 does not name a precondition, rejection rule, or proof/test obligation for `k = 0`.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` under-specifies the context for rooted resolution. `Active attestation` is defined relative to an evaluation time, and `r[web-of-trust.threshold]` explicitly uses `evaluation time t` and says an introducer "resolves as trusted at time `t`". But `r[web-of-trust.rooted-resolution]` defines trust only for subject `S` and depth bound `d`, with no explicit evaluation time or explicit trust-root set parameter, and `r[properties.web-of-trust.depth-monotone]` likewise omits that monotonicity is at fixed time/root set. This is a blocker because the same subject can change status across times or root sets.

Exact-payload semantics depend on a canonical encoding contract that is not specified. `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/proposal.md` says the attestation payload "binds issuer, subject, explicit trust role, validity window, and sequence metadata exactly." In `spec.md`, `r[web-of-trust.attestation-signature]` requires verification over "canonical payload bytes", and `r[web-of-trust.revocation]` requires exact-payload targets to match the attestation's "full canonical signed payload bytes". The spec only fixes `sequence_no` as 8-byte little-endian; it does not define deterministic/injective canonical encoding for issuer, subject, role, validity-window fields, or revocation payload fields. Without that, "changing any signed field MUST invalidate the signature" and exact-payload revocation matching are under-specified.

The `Sequence metadata` definition in `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` calls `sequence_no` "monotone", but no requirement states what must be monotone, over which domain, or whether violations are rejected. No later requirement uses monotonicity. This is either an unsupported stronger claim or a missing requirement, and it should be resolved before design text bakes in the wrong semantics.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` defines **Sequence metadata** as “a monotone unsigned 64-bit `sequence_no`,” and `openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md` Decision 2 repeats “a single monotone `sequence_no: u64`.” But neither artifact defines what monotonicity is checked against, whether it is strict or nondecreasing, or whether non-monotone values are rejected or merely carried as signed metadata. The only concrete semantics presently described are encoding and equality. That leaves acceptance semantics unresolved before tasks or implementation.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md` Decision 2 fixes variable-length byte strings to `u32` little-endian length prefixes and says attestation/revocation payload equality is exact, but `proposal.md`, `design.md`, and `specs/web-of-trust/spec.md` do not state the precondition or failure behavior when `issuer_bytes`, `subject_bytes`, family encodings, or exact-payload target bytes exceed `u32::MAX`. Without an explicit `len <= u32::MAX` rule or rejection contract, the canonical byte format is incomplete and exec/proof `ensures` cannot be exact.

`openspec/changes/web-of-trust-primitives/design.md` Decision 3 makes BLAKE3 and signature verification a plain-Rust crypto boundary, and the Decision 10 table lists `r[verify]` artifacts like “determinism/full-equality proof lemmas” and “exact-payload-binding proof lemmas.” That covers payload construction/use, but it does not name the auditable bridge artifact that carries the trusted contract for the runtime BLAKE3/signature helpers themselves. This is a traceability gap for `r[web-of-trust.principal-fingerprint]` and `r[web-of-trust.attestation-signature]` if those helpers remain outside Verus.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 2 narrows region non-interference to “every writer into the assertion or schedule region must prove non-interference with the other two regions.” But `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` requirement `r[chaoscontrol-coverage.regions]` says “Every helper that writes into one region MUST leave all other regions unaffected.” Code-region writers are not covered by the current design text.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 4 and `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` requirement `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.turns]` both use `min_quantum + (rng_word mod max(max_quantum - min_quantum, 1))`, but neither artifact states a precondition `max_quantum >= min_quantum` nor defines `max_quantum - min_quantum` as mathematical or saturating subtraction. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 8 states `num_nodes <= 64` and that `alive_mask` sets bit `i` iff participant `i` is alive, but it omits the `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` requirement `r[chaoscontrol-fault-state.quorum-health]` constraint that bits above `num_nodes - 1` must stay clear. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/proposal.md` commits to "Verus proofs, unit tests, property tests" under Impact → Testing, but `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/tasks.md` only requires per-module "proofs/tests" plus global commands. The task list has no upfront repo-sync check before implementation. Evidence: `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/tasks.md` starts with adding new modules and ends with validation only. `design.md` does not carry forward all of `r[chaoscontrol-fault-state.quorum-health]`. The spec requires a `num_nodes x num_nodes` partition matrix, `partitioned[i][i] == false`, and that diagonal entries do not contribute to `partition_count` (`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md`, Requirement: Fault-State Quorum Health). `design.md` Decision 8 only states "`partition_count` counts directed blocked links in the asymmetric matrix `partitioned[a][b]`" plus the alive-mask and quorum rule, but does not state matrix shape, diagonal falsity, or diagonal exclusion. That leaves a weaker design than the active spec.

The frontier design leaves exact executable arithmetic under-specified. `design.md` Decision 6 says effective scores use exact rationals and exec code will compare by cross-multiplication, while `spec.md` `r[chaoscontrol-frontier.selection]` requires exact rational ordering. No numeric width, overflow discipline, or proof strategy is specified for the cross-products. Without that, tasks can implement machine-integer comparisons that diverge from the exact spec.

The proposal’s repo-sync preflight is missing from the design plan. `proposal.md` Impact explicitly says: “before implementation, compare this change against `src/lib.rs`, `docs/requirements.md`, `README.md`, and `openspec/specs/` to avoid re-implementing already-shipped scope.” `design.md` Migration Plan starts with adding modules and proofs, but does not include that comparison step. This matches the supplied prior failure pattern and should be promoted into a harder stage rule/check, not left as informal guidance.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/tasks.md` Phase 0 only says to “Compare this change against `src/lib.rs`, `docs/requirements.md`, `README.md`, and `openspec/specs/` to confirm no ChaosControl primitive scope is already shipped elsewhere in the repo”, but it does not define the required next step if that comparison finds overlap. The napkin explicitly calls out this failure pattern: some active changes were already shipped and needed “metadata sync plus archive” rather than new implementation. Several checklist items are broad enough to reduce requirement-level closure visibility against `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md`. Examples: the single `src/chaoscontrol_coverage.rs` task covers `r[chaoscontrol-coverage.regions]`, `r[chaoscontrol-coverage.union]`, and `r[chaoscontrol-coverage.classify]`; the single `src/chaoscontrol_scheduler.rs` task covers both `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.turns]` and `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.fingerprint]`; the single `src/chaoscontrol_fault_state.rs` task covers all of `r[chaoscontrol-fault-state.quorum-health]`. This is not inconsistent, but it makes partial completion and deterministic review harder.

`r[chaoscontrol-fault-state.quorum-health]` is internally inconsistent on its stated domain. The requirement says these primitives apply to `1 <= num_nodes <= 64`, but later says `quorum_reachable` is true only when “some distinct alive pair can reach each other in both directions.” For `num_nodes = 1`, the domain is valid and `majority(1)` is satisfied by one alive node, yet the “distinct alive pair” condition is impossible, so `quorum_reachable` can never be true. Resolve by narrowing the domain or adding a singleton rule. Evidence: `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md`, Requirement `r[chaoscontrol-fault-state.quorum-health]`.

`r[properties.chaoscontrol-quorum-gate]` has no defined implementation target. The proposal promises “every new requirement and `properties.*` rule in this change will map to a concrete defining `r[impl]` artifact,” but the property refers to “A liveness gate derived from the fault-state helper” without any corresponding capability, API, module, or scenario. The proposal only names “predicates used to gate liveness checks” and the capability list stops at `chaoscontrol-fault-state.quorum-health`. This is a traceability blocker. Evidence: `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/proposal.md` under “What Changes”, “Capabilities”, and “Impact > Traceability”; `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md`, Requirement `r[properties.chaoscontrol-quorum-gate]`.

Several requirements restrict valid states but do not specify the public exec API behavior outside those states, even though the proposal’s Impact says this change adds “public spec/exec/proof functions.” Examples: scheduler primitives “apply only when `num_vcpus >= 1`” and ticking is defined only while `remaining > 0`; fault-state helpers “apply only to states with `1 <= num_nodes <= 64`” plus matrix invariants; frontier selection only specifies a “non-empty frontier.” The spec needs to say whether these become Verus `requires`, constructor-enforced invariants, `Option/Result` returns, or defined no-op behavior. Evidence: `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/proposal.md` under “Impact > APIs”; `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md`, Requirements `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.turns]`, `r[chaoscontrol-frontier.selection]`, and `r[chaoscontrol-fault-state.quorum-health]`.

The proposal’s testing note does not fully capture the repo-green workflow called out in the napkin. `proposal.md` lists “Verus proofs, unit tests, property tests, fresh `./scripts/check-ensures.sh`, and fresh `./scripts/verify.sh`,” but not fresh `cargo test`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `./scripts/verus.sh src/lib.rs`, or direct Tracey runs. This should not block proposal approval by itself, but it should be added before later “green tree” claims. Evidence: `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/proposal.md` under “Impact > Testing”; napkin entry on rerunning and capturing fresh command output.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` leaves the scheduler state transition incomplete. `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.turns]` defines countdown, switch signaling, round-robin active-turn advance, and a randomized quantum formula, while `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.fingerprint]` hashes `(active_turn, assigned_quantum)` and defines variant reset. The spec never states what ordinary `advance` does to `remaining`, when `assigned_quantum` is chosen, or how non-random/default quantum reload works after a switch. Design cannot derive the executable state machine or the fingerprint inputs from the current text.

The proposal frames these as deterministic kernels, but the frontier selection requirement admits nondeterministic results. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/proposal.md` says the target kernels are “small deterministic functions,” yet `r[chaoscontrol-frontier.selection]` says “If multiple entries are maximal, any of them may be chosen.” That is a weaker relation than a deterministic helper API and changes reproducibility semantics. Either the proposal must stop claiming deterministic selection, or the spec must define an exact tie-break rule.

`r[chaoscontrol-input-tree.alternatives]` is too weak to encode a concrete alternative-generation kernel. It only requires “at most `b` alternatives” and that each alternative differ from the original while staying in `0 .. n_options`. It does not specify output order, uniqueness, whether duplicates are allowed, or which alternatives must be emitted when the domain exceeds the budget. Under the proposal’s deterministic-kernel framing, many incompatible implementations satisfy the current text.

Fault-schedule normalization and `source_order` are underspecified where replay and subset meet. `r[chaoscontrol-fault-schedule.replay]` defines the stable key as `(time_ns, source_order)` where `source_order` is “the order of the fault in the normalized schedule.” `r[chaoscontrol-fault-schedule.subset]` simultaneously requires duplicate selections to be preserved and the result to be “normalize[d] ... back into the same stable `(time_ns, source_order)` schedule order.” The spec never defines the normalization constructor or how unique `source_order` values are assigned after cloning duplicates, so replay/subset proofs do not have a precise object to target.

The tasks do not explicitly cover the normalized-state boundary that the spec makes part of the contract. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` says public exec/proof APIs operate only on normalized states established by constructors or explicit Verus `requires` clauses, and both `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.turns]` and `r[chaoscontrol-fault-state.quorum-health]` repeat that constructor/`requires`-enforced validity model. `design.md` Decision 4 further requires scheduler validity such as `num_vcpus >= 1` and `remaining > 0` for tick, and Decision 8 requires `2 <= num_nodes <= 64`, exact `num_nodes x num_nodes` shape, and diagonal-false invariants. But `tasks.md` only says to add `src/chaoscontrol_scheduler.rs` and `src/chaoscontrol_fault_state.rs` helpers/proofs/tests; it does not name any task to define or verify constructors, validity predicates, or explicit preconditions for these stateful APIs. That is a traceability gap against the current spec contract and should block implementation planning until tasks name that work.

`design.md` Decision 9 says to reuse existing generic lemmas/modules where possible, specifically calling out `bitmap`, `quorum`, `monotonic`, and `seq_set`, but `tasks.md` contains no checkpoint to evaluate reuse versus duplication or to justify exceptions. This leaves the tasks inconsistent with an explicit design decision and risks drifting into duplicate abstractions.

Several implementation tasks are still broad bundles rather than narrowly checkable units. For example, one checkbox covers all of `src/chaoscontrol_coverage.rs` region constants, merge, classification, new-edge counting, non-interference proofs, unit tests, and property tests; similar bundling appears in the scheduler and fault-state tasks in `tasks.md`. The phase ordering is sensible, but these large aggregates weaken stage-level checkability.

Fault-schedule tie-break semantics are underdefined at the point the design needs to lock them. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` says replay order uses the stable key `(time_ns, source_order)`, "where `source_order` is the order of the fault in the normalized schedule," and subset extraction must normalize clones "back into the same stable `(time_ns, source_order)` schedule order." `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 5 adds that equal-time faults must "stay in source schedule order." None of these artifacts define whether `source_order` is a stored provenance field, the parent normalized index carried through subset extraction, or something recomputed per result. That ambiguity blocks exact proofs for equal-time stability, duplicate preservation, monotone replay order, and `r[properties.chaoscontrol-subset-replay]`.

Frontier exact-rational arithmetic is missing an explicit boundary rule for `1 + times_selected`. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 6 says `base_score` and `times_selected` are `u32` and that exec code will compare candidates with exact `u64` cross-products "without overflow." `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` `r[chaoscontrol-frontier.selection]` also defines the denominator as `1 + times_selected` while allowing `times_selected` to be any `u32`. The design/spec do not state that this addition is performed in mathematical integer / `u64` space, nor do they constrain `times_selected < u32::MAX`. The current text leaves the exactness claim underspecified at the boundary.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 4 gives the fingerprint formula `fp' = fp * 0x517c_c1b7_2722_0a95 ^ active ^ assigned_quantum` but does not state that the mixed `(active, assigned_quantum)` pair is the post-`advance` state. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` under `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.turns]` makes that timing part of the contract: “The `(active_turn, assigned_quantum)` pair used by the fingerprint rule is the post-advance state.” This ambiguity can change the trace definition and fingerprint reproducibility.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 5 models fault schedules as “sorted-by-time sequences plus a cursor” but does not define the normalized state invariant for the cursor itself, such as `0 <= cursor <= len`, nor whether public helpers require normalized schedules only. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` says public APIs operate on normalized states, and `r[chaoscontrol-fault-schedule.replay]` depends on a precise meaning of “not-yet-drained faults.” Without the cursor-bound invariant, replay monotonicity and no-redelivery are underspecified.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 6 defines score ordering and tie-breaks for frontier selection, but it omits the API precondition from `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` `r[chaoscontrol-frontier.selection]`: “The pure greedy-selection helper is defined only for non-empty frontiers.” The design still leaves open whether the exec/proof API requires non-empty input or returns an `Option`/error shape.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 7 states the exact input-tree score `100 / (n_options * (100 + sequence_id))` but does not say how exec code will compare those scores exactly or what arithmetic width keeps the ordering exact. In the same file, Decision 6 explicitly addresses exact rational comparison and overflow for frontier scoring; `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` `r[chaoscontrol-input-tree.alternatives]` requires descending exact-score order. That comparison strategy is still missing for input-tree ranking.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` under `r[chaoscontrol-input-tree.alternatives]` says eligible choices are ordered by descending exact score `100 / (n_options * (100 + sequence_id))`, but it does not define the comparison semantics: exact rational ordering, integer division, or an overflow-safe cross-multiplication rule. `r[chaoscontrol-frontier.selection]` adds that precision explicitly; this requirement does not. Deterministic ordering can diverge without a hard rule.

`r[chaoscontrol-fault-state.quorum-health]` leaves the core predicate underdefined. It uses `majority(n)` without defining it in the supplied artifact, and says quorum is true when “some distinct alive pair can reach each other in both directions,” while the scenario only shows the direct-edge case `!partitioned[a][b]` and `!partitioned[b][a]`. The supplied evidence does not resolve whether “reach” means direct connectivity or transitive path reachability. That changes the intended kernel and proof shape.

`r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.fingerprint]` gives the update `fp' = fp * 0x517c_c1b7_2722_0a95 ^ active_turn ^ assigned_quantum` but does not state the arithmetic domain or overflow behavior. For a verified exec/spec pair, the spec must say whether this is wrapping `u64` arithmetic modulo `2^64` or unbounded integer arithmetic. As written, Rust and Verus implementations can disagree.

The proposal acknowledges the repo-sync check in `proposal.md` Impact (`compare this change against src/lib.rs, docs/requirements.md, README.md, and openspec/specs/`), matching the napkin guidance, but the supplied evidence does not include the actual comparison results. Duplicate-scope risk is therefore still unresolved from evidence.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/tasks.md` task `Add src/chaoscontrol_input_tree.rs with deterministic bounded alternative-generation helpers that preserve domain/original-value invariants plus proofs/unit tests/property tests` does not carry the exact ordering contract from `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` `r[chaoscontrol-input-tree.alternatives]`: eligible choices must be ranked by `100 / (n_options * (100 + sequence_id))`, ties must break by lower `(vm_id, sequence_id)`, and per-choice alternatives must be emitted in ascending order from `0 .. n_options` excluding the original value. `design.md` Decision 7 also fixes that exact score and ordering. As written, the task can be completed while missing stable primitive semantics.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/tasks.md` task `Add src/chaoscontrol_frontier.rs with exact rational effective-score comparison and greedy-selection helpers plus proofs/unit tests/property tests` does not explicitly include two required behaviors from `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` `r[chaoscontrol-frontier.selection]`: monotone decay as `times_selected` increases, and tie-breaking to the lowest input index among maximal candidates. `design.md` Decision 6 fixes first-max scan behavior. The current task text is too loose for exact traceability.

`openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/tasks.md` task `Add src/chaoscontrol_fault_state.rs with constructors/validity predicates or explicit requires-guarded alive-mask, directed partition-count, quorum-reachability, and healthy-period gate helpers plus proofs/unit tests/property tests` leaves the normalized-state constraints from `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` `r[chaoscontrol-fault-state.quorum-health]` implicit: `2 <= num_nodes <= 64`, exact `num_nodes x num_nodes` matrix shape, diagonal entries always `false`, and `alive_mask` bits above `num_nodes - 1` clear. The spec's API Domain says public APIs operate on normalized states established by constructors or explicit `requires` clauses; the task should name those invariants so the state-validity surface is not skipped.

The fault-schedule implementation task does not carry forward several exact compatibility constraints from the spec/design, so the task list is not complete enough for implementation. Evidence: `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` requires in `r[chaoscontrol-fault-schedule.replay]` that schedules are ordered by stable key `(time_ns, ordinal)`, each added fault gets an immutable `ordinal`, draining is monotone and never re-delivers, and in `r[chaoscontrol-fault-schedule.subset]` that subset extraction ignores repeated indices after the first and carries the selected source schedule index as the clone’s `ordinal`. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/tasks.md` only says: “Add `src/chaoscontrol_fault_schedule.rs` with iterative exec code for add/normalize, ordered-drain, subset, and cursor helpers plus proofs/unit tests/property tests,” which omits immutable-ordinal, stable-key, duplicate-index, carried-ordinal, and non-re-delivery specifics.

The input-tree task is missing the task-level guardrail for how exec code preserves the exact rational ranking semantics without float/overflow drift. Evidence: design decision 7 in `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` says exec ranking must use “exact comparison in mathematical integer space or verified no-overflow integer intermediates,” and `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` in `r[chaoscontrol-input-tree.alternatives]` repeats that the implementation may realize the order by exact cross-multiplication or verified no-overflow intermediates. The corresponding task in `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/tasks.md` only says to “rank choices by `100 / (n_options * (100 + sequence_id))`,” with no explicit verification step for the comparison method.

Several task items are broader than the requirement split already established in the delta spec, which weakens stage traceability and completion checks. Evidence: `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` separates `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.turns]` from `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.fingerprint]`, and `r[chaoscontrol-fault-state.quorum-health]` from `r[chaoscontrol-fault-state.liveness-gate]`, but `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/tasks.md` keeps each of those families in one large implementation task. That makes it harder to determine which exact requirement is closed when work starts landing.

The fault-schedule subset contract is incomplete because it never defines the cursor state of the returned schedule, even though replay semantics are cursor-based. Evidence: `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 5 says schedules are modeled as a normalized sequence plus `cursor`, and `drain_due(t)` is defined relative to that cursor. The same decision defines `subset(indices)` only in terms of cloned faults and normalization order. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` `r[chaoscontrol-fault-schedule.subset]` likewise specifies selected faults and stable `(time_ns, ordinal)` normalization but says nothing about the result cursor. `r[properties.chaoscontrol-subset-replay]` then requires replaying an extracted subset. Without an explicit rule such as `cursor = 0` on subset results, replay behavior is under-specified and the cross-module property is not derivable from the current contract.

The input-tree contract leaves the recorded-choice domain under-specified. Evidence: `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 7 and `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` `r[chaoscontrol-input-tree.alternatives]` define choice points only as `(vm_id, sequence_id, n_options, original_value)` and require exact rational ranking plus deterministic alternative generation, but they do not pin numeric types/bounds or define normalized-state constraints such as `original_value < n_options`. The same requirement allows ordering by exact cross-multiplication or “verified no-overflow integer intermediates,” which cannot be planned deterministically without fixed numeric domains. It also leaves “excluding the original value” ambiguous for malformed recorded choices.

`proposal.md` says the change adds verified fault-schedule "`ordering, due-fault draining, cursor monotonicity, and subset extraction`", but `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` only gives `r[chaoscontrol-fault-schedule.replay]` the vague phrase "`behave as a monotone-cursor stream`" plus delivery/no-redelivery semantics. It does not state a concrete cursor invariant or postcondition such as nondecreasing cursor position, cursor advance equaling the number of returned faults, or preservation of the undrained suffix. One advertised capability is therefore not actually encoded yet.

`proposal.md` under **Repo sync** asserts "`current reconnaissance found no existing ChaosControl modules or requirements in those shipped surfaces`", but no evidence from `src/lib.rs`, `docs/requirements.md`, `README.md`, or `openspec/specs/` is supplied here. The napkin explicitly calls this comparison out as a prior failure mode. Treat that statement as unverified until fresh comparison evidence is attached or the text is reduced to a planned pre-implementation check.

`r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.turns]` does not define the public `remaining` state in single-participant mode. The requirement says only, “In single-participant mode, ticking MUST never signal a switch,” and the scenario adds only that “the active participant remains unchanged” and “no tick reports a switch signal.” It does not say whether `remaining` stays constant, decrements, reloads, or is otherwise constrained. Because `remaining` is part of the scheduler state named in the same requirement, this is an underspecified transition contract that can produce incompatible designs.

The scheduler spec leaves randomized-mode initial/reset quantum semantics unresolved. `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.turns]` says the initial state “MUST start at active participant `0` with `remaining = max(1, quantum)`,” while randomized assignment later says assigned quantum “MUST use the existing ChaosControl lower-inclusive, upper-exclusive rule `min_quantum + (rng_word mod max(max_quantum - min_quantum, 1))`.” `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.fingerprint]` then says applying a new schedule variant resets `remaining` to `max(1, quantum_override.unwrap_or(default_quantum))`. The current text does not say whether the first turn in randomized mode, or the first turn after variant application, uses a sampled quantum or the scalar default/override value. That ambiguity affects both exec behavior and proof obligations.

Scheduler state transitions are not fully specified for the exact deterministic contract the change claims. In `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/design.md` Decision 4, the scheduler state includes `rng_state`, randomized assignment uses `next_rng`, and `apply_variant` "reseeds RNG", but there is no rule for how `rng_state` produces `next_rng` or when `rng_state` advances. The same decision and `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` `r[chaoscontrol-scheduler.turns]` only constrain single-participant mode to "never signal a switch" and do not define what happens to exposed state such as `remaining` in that mode. This is a gap against `proposal.md` "deterministic vCPU scheduling" and design text claiming "exact upstream transitions"; tasks cannot implement or verify seeded scheduler reproducibility from the current contract.

The required repo-sync audit is only deferred, not evidenced. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/proposal.md` under **Impact** says "before implementation, compare this change against `src/lib.rs`, `docs/requirements.md`, `README.md`, and `openspec/specs/`", and `design.md` Migration Plan step `0` repeats that requirement, but no artifact in this change records the audit result. Given the breadth of scope (`src/chaoscontrol_*.rs` modules plus `src/properties.rs` and docs updates), overlap with already-shipped code remains unresolved. This matches the supplied napkin failure pattern and should be treated as a hard pre-work gate, not optional guidance.

The tasks apply the normalized-state contract inconsistently across modules. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` says in **API Domain** that public exec/proof APIs operate on normalized states established by constructors or explicit Verus `requires` clauses. `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/tasks.md` carries that forward for scheduler (`"constructors/validity predicates or explicit \`requires\`-guarded tick/advance logic"`) and fault state (`"constructors/validity predicates or explicit \`requires\`-guarded invariants"`), but not for coverage or fault schedule. The coverage task only says `"Add \`src/chaoscontrol_coverage.rs\` with exact 64 KiB region constants..."` even though `r[chaoscontrol-coverage.regions]` requires a 64 KiB bitmap. The fault-schedule task only says `"Add \`src/chaoscontrol_fault_schedule.rs\` with iterative exec code for immutable ordinals, \`(time_ns, ordinal)\` normalization, cursor bounds..."` even though `r[chaoscontrol-fault-schedule.replay]` requires a normalized stream with `0 <= cursor <= len`. Add explicit constructor/validity or `requires` work items for these modules before implementation starts.

Some tasks are too coarse relative to the spec requirements they are meant to close. In `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/tasks.md`, one fault-schedule task bundles replay ordering, cursor advance, non-re-delivery, subset duplicate suppression, carried ordinals, `cursor = 0`, proofs, unit tests, and property tests, while `openspec/changes/chaoscontrol-primitives/specs/chaoscontrol/spec.md` separates that scope into `r[chaoscontrol-fault-schedule.replay]` and `r[chaoscontrol-fault-schedule.subset]`.
